facts: Spain has around 48 million people, making it one of the largest consumer markets in the EU and a market where regional strategy beats one-size-fits-all national campaigns.
Google is by far the leading search engine in Spain, so Spanish SEO is Google SEO, with no significant local engine to split the effort.
Spain is an early adopter of Google's AI Overviews, which appear in 14 to 16 percent of desktop searches, so content here needs to be structured for both classic rankings and AI answers.
PaginasAmarillas, published by QDQ Media, is Spain's legacy business directory and still a recognized citation source for local SEO.
Spain's privacy framework pairs the EU GDPR with the national LOPDGDD law (Ley Organica 3/2018), enforced by the AEPD, which affects consent banners, forms and tracking setups.
Tourism is one of Spain's biggest industries and it is intensely seasonal, which makes seasonal SEO planning a core skill for businesses on the coasts and islands.
Madrid and Barcelona are the two business capitals, with Valencia, Seville, Bilbao, Malaga and Zaragoza as strong regional hubs, each with its own search behavior.
Spanish is the world's second most spoken native language, which means a strong Spanish SEO foundation can later extend into Latin American markets.

h1: SEO Expert in Spain: Turn Spanish Searches into Paying Customers
intro:
Spain rewards businesses that understand Spain. Forty-eight million people, two business capitals in Madrid and Barcelona, strong regional hubs in Valencia, Seville, Bilbao, Malaga and Zaragoza, and a tourism industry that rewires search demand every single year. The businesses winning Spanish search results are not the ones with the biggest budgets. They are the ones whose websites speak to Spanish buyers the way Spanish buyers actually think: in Spanish, with Spanish reviews, Spanish hours, and an understanding that a customer in Barcelona does not behave exactly like a customer in Seville.

Language is the first thing outsiders get wrong. Spanish dominates commercial search nationwide, and that will not surprise you. What surprises people is how much the regional languages matter commercially. In Catalonia, a meaningful share of local searches happens in Catalan, and businesses that serve Barcelona in Catalan earn trust that Spanish-only competitors do not. Basque and Galician play the same role in their regions. This is not a political statement; it is search behavior. I research which languages your customers actually type in, then build each language as its own deliberate effort with its own keyword research, never as an afterthought translation.

The second thing outsiders get wrong is rhythm. Spain runs on seasons. The coasts, the islands, the cities with festival calendars: demand surges and falls on a timetable, and SEO has a lead time. A restaurant in Marbella that starts thinking about summer rankings in May has already lost. The winners do the work in the quiet months. I plan every tourism-adjacent campaign backwards from the booking window, so content, profiles and reviews are in place before demand arrives.

Google is by far the leading search engine here, which keeps the technical playbook focused. Spain is also an early adopter of AI Overviews, appearing in 14 to 16 percent of desktop searches, so content needs to win classic rankings and earn AI citations at the same time. I am a one-person studio: you work directly with me, the audit is free, and the strategy is built around how Spaniards search, compare and buy. Not a translated template. A Spain playbook. A final note on working with me: I am a one-person studio, so the person who audits your site is the person who fixes it. Spanish business owners tell me they are tired of agencies that sell in January and disappear by March. My model is the opposite: direct contact, monthly plain-language reports, and work you can verify yourself in the search results. The free audit is genuinely free, and it will show you exactly where you stand before you spend anything.

section1.body:
Spanish citations have a local flavor that generic citation campaigns miss. Google cross-checks your business details across the web, and in Spain that check runs through PaginasAmarillas, the legacy directory published by QDQ Media, alongside Yelp, TripAdvisor for hospitality, Facebook, and your Google Business Profile. PaginasAmarillas will not send you customers directly anymore, but Google treats it as an established Spanish trust source, so a correct listing there supports everything else. The pattern I see constantly: Spanish businesses with five slightly different listings across these directories, each with a different phone format, an old address, or a name spelled three ways.

My citation process for Spain is methodical. First, the Google Business Profile: claimed, verified, fully completed with categories that match Spanish search terms, services, attributes, real photos, and hours that reflect Spanish reality, including midday breaks where they apply. Wrong hours are uniquely costly in Spain because 'abierto ahora' filtering is heavily used; a customer who filters for open-now businesses never sees you if your hours are wrong. Second, I audit and fix the directory footprint: PaginasAmarillas claimed and corrected, Yelp, TripAdvisor where relevant, sector directories for your trade. Every listing ends up with the same +34 number in the same format, the same address, the same business name.

Then comes the layer that matters most in Spain: reviews in Spanish, replied to in Spanish. Spanish buyers read reviews before they call, before they visit, before they book, and they notice whether the business replies. A profile with recent Spanish reviews and thoughtful Spanish replies converts at a completely different rate than a silent one. I build the review routine into your operation: the right ask after the service, a direct link, replies within a day. Citations get you into the map pack conversation; reviews win it. In Spain, I treat them as one system, because Spanish buyers do. For hospitality and tourism businesses I add TripAdvisor to the citation core, because it doubles as a review platform Spanish travelers trust. The principle stays the same: identical details everywhere, claimed profiles, no duplicates. Spanish directories are fewer than in some markets, which makes each one count more.
section1.heading: Citations and Directories: Spain's Local Footprint

section2.body:
The map pack decides local business in Spain. For searches like 'fontanero Madrid', 'dentista Barcelona' or 'restaurante cerca de mi', Google shows three businesses before any website, and the customer picks from those three. Spanish map pack competition in Madrid and Barcelona is fierce, while regional cities offer faster wins. Either way, the profile that wins is the one that looks alive: complete information, recent reviews, real photos, fresh posts, answered questions.

Spanish profile optimization has details that matter. Categories need to match Spanish search phrasing. Attributes need attention: Spaniards filter by them. The Q&A section should be seeded with the questions customers actually ask, answered in Spanish, because unanswered questions invite competitors or random users to answer for you. Posts should show current offers, seasonal menus, real updates, not generic stock content. And photos need to be real: the premises, the team, the work. Spanish buyers have a finely tuned sense for stock photography, and it costs trust.

Reviews are the tiebreaker, and Spain has a strong review culture. Volume, recency, rating and replies all feed the map pack algorithm, but just as importantly they feed the human decision. A 4.6-star profile with eighty recent Spanish reviews and replies to all of them will take the call from a 4.9-star profile with nine silent reviews. I make review generation systematic: QR codes, direct links by WhatsApp or SMS after the job, replies in Spanish within 24 hours. Negative reviews get calm, specific, solution-focused replies, because in Spain a well-handled complaint often converts better than another five-star praise. The map pack is a three-way contest. I optimize your profile to win it. One more Spanish-specific detail: WhatsApp. A huge share of Spanish customer contact happens over WhatsApp, so your profile and website should make messaging you effortless. I add click-to-chat paths where they make sense and make sure your phone number is consistent everywhere, because in Spain the call often starts as a WhatsApp message.

why.body:
Spain looks like a straightforward market until you try to win it with a generic playbook. The first thing that breaks is language strategy. Spanish covers most commercial searches, but Catalonia is the exception that proves you need local knowledge: a real share of Barcelona searches happen in Catalan, and businesses that serve the city in Catalan earn a trust premium. Basque and Galician matter the same way in their regions. Agencies that run 'Spanish SEO' as a single national campaign either ignore this and leave money on the table, or machine-translate and embarrass the brand. I treat each language as its own market with its own research.

The second thing that breaks is timing. Spain's economy breathes in seasons. Coastal tourism, island tourism, city festivals, ski in the Pyrenees: demand follows a calendar, and SEO follows a lead time of months. A campaign that ignores seasonality builds the wrong content at the wrong time and wonders why summer never came. I have watched tourism businesses spend all winter on brand content and start thinking about booking keywords in May, which is like training for a marathon the week before. My Spain campaigns are planned backwards from the season, every time.

The third thing is buyer behavior. Spanish customers are thorough. They check Maps, read reviews in Spanish, compare photos, and filter by 'abierto ahora' before they move. They are also loyal once won: a Spanish customer who trusts you returns and recommends. That means your online presence has to survive scrutiny, not just attract a click. Thin profiles, unanswered reviews, stock photos and wrong hours do not just cost rankings here; they cost the customer at the decision moment. The Spain playbook I run respects all three realities: real language strategy, seasonal timing, and a presence built to survive a careful buyer's inspection. There is a fourth reality worth naming: Spain's SEO market itself is still maturing. Industry surveys have found that only about a third of Spanish companies prepare proper SEO strategies, which means most of your competitors are improvising. Against improvisation, a real strategy wins quickly. That is the gap I exploit for clients here.
